dossier.summary: On the eight-case synthetic grid, the frozen exposure library has lower mean relative RMSE than linear regression, while two-hop error remains large and nominal intervals undercover. The delivered source, result registry and recorded evaluation jobs support these numerical findings, and the PDF matches the LaTeX source. The study does not isolate why the library improves performance or provide a per-case bias–variance decomposition or paired uncertainty for its main comparison. Its limitations are mostly stated explicitly, and the final evaluation tests new seeds of the same mechanism families rather than new mechanisms. Reproduction would benefit from complete run instructions, figure dependencies and retained per-instance outputs; gaps in the process record leave historical access to evaluation truth uncertain.

claims.quote: A frozen estimator that selects among 15 low-parameter exposure mappings with a BIC gate reaches a mean relative RMSE of 0.126, against 0.180 for plain linear exposure regression, 0.622 for difference-in-means, 0.994 for a neighbourhood Horvitz--Thompson estimator, and 0.045 for an oracle regression given the true mapping.

Per-case error is 0.031--0.054 in the five cases whose generating form is linear in the neighbour-treated fraction, across three graph families, a threefold change in interference strength and both assignment designs, and 0.151--0.452 in the saturating, count-by-degree and two-hop cases.
Nominal 95\% intervals cover only 0.839 of the time.

We hypothesize that exposure-mapping mismatch and extrapolation to the all-treated and all-control corners drive the larger errors; this account is consistent with the single-factor contrasts but untested, because the grid is not factorial and the selected mappings were not verified.
two other estimator classes (a flexible ridge ensemble and a linear model with a design-weighted residual correction) scored worse than the gated library on the model-selection seeds.
A transparent, scale-free protocol (relative RMSE per case, averaged over cases) with four reference estimators and three negative controls.

issues.quote: we did not run a paired test.
issues.why: The main RMSE comparison has no dispersion or paired interval. The bootstrap interval concerns the studied estimator's mean absolute error, a different statistic, and cannot quantify the RMSE improvement over the baseline; this limitation is explicitly acknowledged.

issues.quote: No ablation of the gate margin or library components was run.
issues.why: Neither the gate nor an individual mapping is isolated, and selected mappings are unrecorded. The proposed explanation for the improvement and two-hop failure therefore remains untested, as the paper explicitly concedes.

issues.quote: Per-case bias is not recorded, so a substantial systematic component exists on average but is not shown to be concentrated in the cases with higher error.
issues.why: The ratio of mean absolute bias to mean RMSE is not a bias–variance decomposition: squared bias and variance must be evaluated within cases before aggregation. No estimator variance by case or scaling with graph size is reported, leaving the task's error-composition question only partly answered.

issues.quote: The HT reference is design-based, whereas the regression estimators accept model risk in exchange for using every unit.
issues.why: The HT implementation uses only closed one-hop neighborhoods even for two-hop outcomes, and in the cluster design sets contributions to zero when a neighborhood spans more than five blocks and has zero exposure probability (evaluate.py:881–911). This limits its interpretation as a GATE reference; the paper already qualifies it as untuned and avoids a general superiority claim.

issues.quote: Case specifications are shared between model selection and final scoring, and the library was developed after the two earlier estimator classes had been scored on the model-selection seeds; the final result is out-of-sample over seeds but not over mechanisms.
issues.why: The library includes the exact generating sigmoid and was developed using results on these same mechanism families. New seeds support replication within the grid, but there is no evidence for transfer to mechanisms outside that library; the paper states this limitation.

presentation.why: Many labels in Figure 1's feature boxes and case grid are only a few pixels high in the prescribed 100-dpi page render; its detailed annotations are difficult to read at printed-page scale.
The main method description prints source_evidence paths, Python filenames and function names. Similar implementation traces recur on pages 5 and 8 and interrupt the scientific description.
The last appendix paragraph spills only three lines onto an otherwise empty final page.

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: We also report the mean over cases of the absolute mean signed relative error (``bias''),
paper_mismatches.why: The implementation clips signed relative errors to [-2,2] before averaging, while the stated bias definition does not mention clipping. This does not affect the reported final bias: every final per-seed mean capped absolute error is below 0.25 across eight cases, ruling out any individual error reaching the cap.

problems.why: Appendix A.6 lists sources, seeds and dependencies, but supplies no complete evaluation invocation or instructions identifying the frozen estimator path. No top-level README.md or REPRODUCE.md is delivered.
build_figures.py imports matplotlib at line 6, but the delivered requirements.txt lists only numpy, scipy, scikit-learn and networkx; the figure environment is not fully specified.

The final results are embedded in paper_data.json as aggregate metrics and per-seed mean errors. Per-instance estimates, truths, intervals and mapping choices are not retained, so paired baseline uncertainty and per-case bias/variance cannot be reconstructed from the delivered summaries.

process_notes: Counts refer to the entries in tables.json, not individual seeds or case evaluations. Experiments comprise one baseline calibration command, three selection jobs and the final evaluation; smoke and qualification jobs are checks.

failed_then_fixed counts the three failures explicitly marked recovered in tables.json. Some shell commands returned success after an inner process failed, so this is not a complete count of transient failures.

All 384 indexed commands were opened in trajectory.json, including comparison outputs and evaluator edits. fields.json records missing command histories for five sessions; no absence-of-work finding is inferred from those gaps.

integrity.why: The recorded adaptive comparisons use selection seeds 101–108. The selected library then has one final job on seeds 9001–9024; the delivered manifests have no cross-set graph or graph/assignment/outcome hash overlap. Selection-set values are explicitly labeled as such in Table 3; no final-score-driven method choice is shown.

The visible evaluator edits concern initial implementation, replay aggregation and subprocess fixes before estimator comparisons. Selection and final evaluators differ only in plane designation, seeds and budgets, and the final evaluator matches the recorded hash; no undisclosed change favoring a reported result is shown.

The inspected estimator receives observed outcomes but not the counterfactual GATE or mechanism, and visible development reads concern selection results. However, fields.json reports five sessions without command transcripts, so the complete history of access to evaluation truth cannot be established; generating truth inside the evaluator is not itself leakage.

The reported selection numbers correspond to three completed evaluation jobs, final metrics to the completed final job, and derived statistics to recorded analysis/figure invocations. No reported quantity was found to require an absent experiment or a hand-entered result.
